text: Τὴν ἀθανασίαν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀφῃρημένοις. Sic ambo Gregorii aliique sancti Aristotelem trahunt in opinionem mortalitatis animorum, quorum certe magna fides est et auctoritas, pro eorum in Græcis Aristotelis atque ejus dogmatis diligentia. Qui utique, si conciliare Aristotelem licuisset, amicum maluissent, quam ut sibi ac catholicæ fidei, in re tanti, tantum adversarium committerent. Ejus ἐνδελέχεια, actusque et perfectio corporis, velut est acuties in ferro, de hominis animo eoque immortali non satis congruat : sanctus doctor tamen serio laboravit vindicando Aristotelem, et ut ejus sanam mentem in opinione de anima immortali assereret : quæ tractatio longam lucubrationem exposceret ; quæ proinde alterius operæ et otii sit. Rite autem Maximus, ex negatione actus proprii et insignientis, qui in anima rationali, actus ipse rationis est, ut scilicet intelligat et velit, ipsius animæ negationem ac interitum colligit : ut perinde sit, sic inertem esse, ac non esse. Quod monachorum, et in illis celebriorum, fuisse hunc errorem deplorat Maximus, hoc admonet, monachos qui simpliciores minusque eruditi sunt, proclivius errore labi, eoque semel imbibito, fere capitosiores esse, qua sibi blandiuntur sanctitatis larva potius, quam ipsa veritate. Atque utinam Maximi hæc duntaxat tempora contingerent, ac, vel quibus ex munere indicta studiorum necessitas, serio illis secundum pietatem navarent operam, non sæculari ambitu turbas fratribus facerent, omniumque diris devoti, mulierculárum favore omni modo comitatui vim facerent, ut majores prælati et antistites, invitis sacris canonibus Patrumque institutis, fierent, qui nec minora replere subsellia, exigui meritis ac scientia nullaque modestia (ut mitissime dicam) digni exsistant !
en: Thus both Gregories and other saints draw Aristotle into the opinion that souls are mortal; their faith and authority are certainly great, given their diligence in the Greek Aristotle and his teaching. They would surely, had it been possible to reconcile Aristotle, have preferred him as a friend rather than set so great an adversary against themselves and the catholic faith. His entelechy, the actuality and perfection of the body, like the sharpness in iron, does not sufficiently fit man's soul, and an immortal one; yet the holy doctor laboured earnestly in defending Aristotle and in asserting that his sound meaning lay in the opinion on the immortal soul; that treatment would demand long labour, and belongs to another work and leisure. Rightly, then, Maximus, from the negation of the proper and distinguishing act, which in the rational soul is reason itself, namely that it understand and will, infers the negation and perishing of the soul itself, so that it is the same to be inert as not to be. That Maximus laments this error as having been among monks, and the more famous of them, warns that the simpler and less learned monks slip into error more readily and, once it is imbibed, are generally more stubborn, since they flatter themselves with a mask of holiness rather than the truth. And would that only the times of Maximus had such things befall, and that those on whom study was imposed by their office would earnestly devote themselves to it according to piety, not make disturbances for the brothers by worldly ambition, and, cursed by all, by the favour of little women force their way in every manner into the company, so that they become greater prelates and bishops against the sacred canons and institutions of the Fathers, who are unworthy even to fill the lesser seats, of small merit and learning and (to put it mildly) no modesty!

text: Τοῦ αὐτοῦ. Unus Regius cod. Τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐπιστολὴ ἄλλη, περὶ ἀγάπης : quæ additio περὶ ἀγάπης superflua, respuuntque alii codices. Num et τὸ, πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν, additicium sit variantibus codicibus, pronuntiare non ausim. Quod καλὸν ποιμένα καὶ διδάσκαλον, Pastorem et magistrum vocat, etiam in presbyterum congruit, qualis erat Jordanis, qui forte ipse hegumenus, sive monasterio præfectus erat, sub quo Maximus vel meruerat, vel ejus imbutus doctrina fuerat : etsi in episcopum aptius foret, qui ipse simpliciter pastor, ac cujus præcipue muneris docere sit ; etsi illi utraque functione minores sacerdotes (parochi maxime, fratresque Mendicantes juris communis dispositione illis partim consenti, nec paucis æquati) adjutores sint : neutri ita spernendi, utrique fovendi, ut ipso hierarcha summoque duce, velut acies ordinata consurgat, cui præest, Christiana, ipsa perficiens, præsidensque ac regens, vel in ipso foro fori, vel solo animæ foro quasi tribunis suis et centurionibus, præter imperatorem suum, instructa hierarchia ; uno summo hierarcha Petri successore, omnes sibi hierarchas, subditasque illis plebes, necnon muneris adjutores (ipsos vicaria eis opera προστάτας, secundi nimirum ordinis sacerdotes) uniente, ut sit una columba, una sponsa, una et acies, una Ecclesia : extra quam quidquid est, profanum est, nec in Ecclesiæ computandum censum, sed παρασυναγωγῆς et conventiculi Satanæ.
anchorLine: Η'. — Τοῦ αὐτοῦ (k) πρὸς τὸν αὐτόν.
en: One royal codex has: 'Of the same. Another letter, on love'; this addition 'on love' is superfluous, and other codices reject it. Whether 'to the same' too is a later addition to the variant readings I would not dare to pronounce. That he calls him 'good shepherd and teacher', 'Pastor and teacher', also fits a presbyter, such as Jordanis was, who perhaps was himself hegumen or head of a monastery, under whom Maximus either had served or been steeped in his teaching; though it would fit a bishop better, who is simply a shepherd and whose chief office is to teach; and though lesser priests (chiefly parish priests, and the Mendicant friars, partly by common-law provision, and not a few put on a par) are their helpers in each function: neither is to be despised, both are to be fostered, so that the Christian host, ordered as a battle line, may arise with the supreme hierarch as leader, whom it follows, itself accomplishing the work, presiding and ruling, whether in the very forum of the court or in the sole forum of the soul, as with its tribunes and centurions, apart from its emperor, with the hierarchy drawn up; with one supreme hierarch, successor of Peter, uniting to himself all the hierarchs, the people subject to them, and the helpers of the office (the 'presidents' who act for them, priests of the second order), so that there be one dove, one bride, one host, one Church: outside which whatever exists is profane, and not to be counted in the Church's reckoning, but is a 'gathering aside' and conventicle of Satan.
